task_reviews.review_summary: Both witness and key identify nominative king as giver, dative singular man as recipient and accusative feminine book as gift. Syncretic menn is not misread as plural. Both identify hie as accusative feminine singular book. Object role and grammatical gender, not human reference, determine the analysis. Both retain genuine king/man ambiguity of masculine singular he. Neither imposes nearest-noun reference. Both rewrite only the second sentence as Se mann hie raedde, explicitly naming the prior recipient as reader.

Both identify the quoted ic as king and the seeing as earlier than the statement. Witness and key independently give Se cyning saegde thaet he thone mann gesawe. The requested reporting verb, content clause, third-person king reference and past subjunctive are all retained. Both distinguish reported mood from truth/falsity and from automatic anterior tense. No false-report inference is required.

Both translate the men as seers and singers, with the king only the person seen. Both assign subject function to relative the and plural agreement to both gesawon and sungon; accusative king controls neither. Both change subject and both finite verbs to Se mann ... geseah, sang while retaining singular accusative king.
Witness and key agree on the complete sentence: main man gives; relative king sees; relative object man, dative servant and accusative book remain distinct.
Witness and key agree on hatan plus accusative plural actors and plain sellan, with separate dative servant and accusative plural books.

Identical singular subject/object and haefth; weak assa remains nominative, not oblique assan. Identical assan/saccas/habbath plural contrast; both noun classes and finite agreement are correct. Witness places wheat before recipients; key places recipients first. Both have nominative plural menn, sellath, mass accusative hwaete and dative plural assum. Order is unrestricted. Identical singular wheat and is with static on plus dative plural saccum; container plurality does not alter subject agreement. Both explain weak -an versus strong -as and shared dative -um in recipients/location; witness also correctly distinguishes irregular menn and mass wheat.

Identical third-singular present bethearf and governed genitive hwaetes. Identical third-plural preterite bethorfton and unchanged genitive mass complement. Both explain tense, subject-number agreement and selected genitive government independently; no plural wheat inference.

Identical first-singular present oncnāwe with accusative singular king. Identical first-plural preterite oncnēowon with unchanged singular object. Identical third-singular present undēth and singular sack object. Identical plural subject/object and preterite undydon; present and past stems are not conflated. Both separate finite agreement/tense changes from object number and noun/article changes; neither lets the nearer object control the verb.

No dael lexical hint is imposed by Cook. Initial key wrongly called Jacob king; A03 corrects that speaker explanation.

Witness rearranges gifts/pronoun naturally in English without reversing antecedents. Complete independent translation agrees on narrated guest departures, two addressed dignitaries, two distinct him referents and the proposed going/seeking/rest. Both identify princess as new first-person giver and Apollonius as dative recipient, after the king’s speech ends. Both distinguish singular Apollonius recipient from plural servant addressees, with postposed to in the latter clause.

Both distinguish daughter as geseah subject from her heart as gefēoll subject; source singular agreement is retained. Both distinguish genitive plural weight-unit after two hundred from genitive singular material gold. Quantity help remains visible. Both use original note13: menn is antecedent/relative subject, hie gifts are relative object, giefa is main-clause object. The separated relative is not attached to the gifts. Both distinguish accusative plural gesunde with infinitival actor hie from nominative plural gesunde with subject ge in direct wish; identical spelling does not merge constructions.

Both identify temporal frame containing a seeing-content clause, followed by main falling-in-love event; indicative source forms preserved. Both distinguish permission-content thaet ic moste from free-choice gift relatives, earlier wolde from current second-singular wille, and permission from obligation. Both identify first-plural exhortation gan we, seeking infinitive and final purpose with maegen plus infinitive gerestan/reflexive accusative us. Completion is not asserted.

Both identify father’s earlier and renewed authority and princess’s selection/enumeration of the gifts. No unsupported individual royal prescriptions. Both distinguish guests already home from Apollonius’s next proposed action; seeking lodging, arrival and rest remain unnarrated at boundary177.2.
